# Expansion of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization: a platform for regional cooperation or a tool for power projection?

## ABSTRACT

Since 2015, the number of full member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) has expanded from six to ten countries. In the 2020s, the withdrawal of the US from Afghanistan and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have altered the regional security landscape and economic conditions. The usefulness of the SCO has been demonstrated in its inward-looking security aspects, such as counter-terrorism and regime security. The objective of this paper is to examine the characteristics and changes in regional cooperation within the expanded SCO. The main arguments of this paper are as follows: First, the inward-looking regional cooperation that has driven the SCO since its establishment remains intact. Second, while a non-Western economic space that can circumvent economic sanctions is emerging between the new full member states and China and Russia, there is competition over the integration of Afghanistan. Third, following the withdrawal of the US troops from Afghanistan, the stabilization of Afghanistan has resurfaced as a priority for both the founding members and the new members of the SCO. In particular, competition between China and Russia has intensified over political and economic influence in Afghanistan. Russia’s decline and a rivalry between India and China could be issues of concern for the balance of power and cohesion within the SCO.

## 1. Introduction

The Russo-Ukrainian War has dragged on for more than three years by the time of writing this paper and a restructuring of the international security order is taking place in Russia’s neighboring regions. In Europe, Finland and Sweden have joined the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) in response to the Russian military threat, whereas in Asia, North Korea has formed a military alliance with Russia and supports Russian military operations both in Kursk region and Eastern part of Ukraine. Meanwhile, Eurasian countries that are not members of the European Union (EU) and have no military alliance with the United States are increasingly applying to join the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). Currently, the 10 full members of the SCO include major non-Western countries and nuclear powers such as Russia, China, India, and Pakistan. Iran (2023) and Belarus (2024) have also recently gained full membership. Furthermore, since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, six Middle Eastern Countries have become dialogue partners with the SCO. What factors have attracted non-Western countries to the SCO since the late 2010s?

Before Xi Jinping announced the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2013, Beijing hoped to develop the SCO as an instrument in promoting multilateral economic cooperation. Yet, after Russia blocked China’s initiatives such as the creation of a development bank and free trade zones, Beijing began to expand its economic relations with Central Asian countries independently under the BRI as well as the China-Central Asia Summit. Footnote 1 Since February 2022, however, Russian banks have been banned from the Swift financial network. Under such circumstances, Russia and China have taken the lead in the “de-dollarization” of trade in particular with BRICS members to build an alternative economic architecture to the dominance of the US dollar. In October 2024, Russian President Vladimir Putin said in response to questions from the leading media of the BRICS countries that the ruble and yuan are used in 95% of Russia’s transactions with China. Footnote 2 Thus, recently, economic cooperation and the de-dollarization of international payments have been promoted outside the SCO.

Regarding the unique and sustained role of the SCO, until the 2010s, a leading expert assessed that Russia viewed the SCO as a political organization rather than an economic one and planned to strengthen military and political cooperation through the Collective Security Organization (CSTO). Footnote 3 Studies focusing on regional cooperation among the six original full members prior to expansion argue that the SCO fundamentally focuses on the regime security and maintenance of the current, authoritarian leadership in power. Footnote 4 In this sense, as Steven Aris points out, the SCO is driven by internal concerns of regime security among its members and is not a military bloc against the West. Footnote 5 As for the external functions of the SCO, Roy Allison points out that the protective integration functions of the SCO are expressed in solidarity through resisting externally “imposed” norms or rallying against pressure for democratic processes and good governance. Footnote 6 These prior studies reveal that SCO members have sought to achieve and enhance the dual functions through the SCO: strengthening domestic governance within member countries while simultaneously preventing or rejecting the penetration of influence by external actors that threaten authoritarian regimes.

Over the past decade, from 2015 to the present, the SCO has expanded largely in South Asia and the Middle East. Today, many of the twenty-six countries including observers and dialogue partners, are non-Western countries classified as authoritarian states. Footnote 7 How has the participation of new full members – India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus – affected the dual functions of the SCO described above? The primary purpose of this paper is to reexamine the centripetal force and solidarity against the external threats of the SCO after its expansion by examining the motives for joining of the four new full members. Second, this paper discusses the impact of the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the competition among the US, Russia, and China for power projection over Central Asian states and Afghanistan.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: The second section explains the objectives of the Shanghai Five, the predecessor of the SCO, and the background behind the SCO’s focus on the “three evils” of terrorism, separatism, and extremism. It also explains the characteristics of the SCO in relation to the US and examines how it has sought to ensure solidarity in its external relations. The third section reevaluates the attractiveness and usefulness of the SCO by analyzing the background of the full membership of India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus, taking into consideration their economic interests and geopolitical positions. The fourth section discusses the impact of the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the regional security landscape and the solidarity of SCO members.

### 2.1. From confidence building in border areas to the fight against “three evils”

The roots of regional security cooperation among Russia, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and China lie in the negotiations on border problems between the USSR and China that were resumed in November 1989, following the historic normalization of Sino-Soviet relation in May 1989. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the negotiations on border problems between the USSR and China were transferred to a multilateral framework involving Russia and the three newly independent states in Central Asia and China. The term “Shanghai Five” was first used at a summit meeting held in Shanghai in April 1996. The Shanghai Five signed an agreement on confidence-building in the military field in border areas in 1996 and an agreement on mutual reduction of military forces in border areas in 1997. Footnote 8 

In the late 1990s, the common concern of these five countries was, first, ensuring security in the border regions between China and the other four countries. Second, counter-terrorism emerged as a common concern. Originally, the Afghanistan issue was not a major agenda item for the Shanghai Five. Footnote 9 In the mid-1990s, when the Islamic extremist movement began, the Taliban assumed state power of Afghanistan and the security situation in the neighboring Central Asian states largely deteriorated by directly facing the threat of terrorism and the problems of illegal trafficking of drugs and weapons. For Russia’s national security, religious extremism in Central Asia remains intertwined with unrest and conflict in the Caucasus, including Chechnya. Meanwhile, for China, relations with Central Asia and Afghanistan are closely linked not only to the stability of its border regions, but also to territorial integrity, the protection of national unity, the fight against transnational crime, and stability in the northwest. In particular, the fight against the “three evils” of terrorism, extremism, and separatism is linked to China’s fight against the East Turkistan independence movement in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

In such a regional context, after most of the borders between China and the other four countries were demarcated by the beginning of the twenty-first century, fighting against terrorism, separatism, extremism was upgraded to the basic driving force for the establishment of the SCO in June 2001. Footnote 10 The founding members of this organization are the above five countries and Uzbekistan.

### 2.2. From pro-US to the removal of US military presence

Researchers outside the SCO region are inclined to view the SCO as an international organization aimed at countering the US and NATO. However, from the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001 up to 2005, the depth and scope of US access to Central Asia reached historically unprecedented levels. The SCO member states decided to actively cooperate with the United States, motivated by the desire to grant international legitimacy to their “fight against terrorism.” Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan accepted the stationing of US troops at Karshi-Khanabad and Manas airbases for logistics and supply, respectively. Tajikistan also allowed the US Air Force planes to refuel at the Ayni air base near Dushanbe after the 9/11 attacks. However, in 2014, the Kyrgyz government under President Kurmanbek Bakiyev decided to close the Manas Air Base (officially labeled the Transit Centre at Manas), which had served as a key logistics hub for the US military operations in Afghanistan. As a result, the US lost all of its military bases in Central Asia. On the one hand, this decision has been attributed to pressure from Russia and China to reduce U.S. military presence. On the other hand, authorities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan viewed the frequent anti-government movements (so-called “color revolutions”) in the former Soviet region, including their own countries, as being supported by Western countries, and sought to rethink their relations with the United States. In this context, as described below, this can be seen as an example of a small country using policy coordination within an international organization like the SCO to amplify its voice. Footnote 11
